decisions.reason: Under Codebook Step 2, a target must be a study whose published empirical finding is re-tested rather than a work supplying the assay/task or background comparisons. Fiske et al. (2019) adopt the multiple-schedule reinforcer assessment (MSA) procedure from Smaby et al. (2007; 10.1002/bin.242, shipped and base-blind target 0) and the star-pointing task and fixed sequence from Cividini-Motta and Ahearn (2013; 10.1002/jaba.67, base-blind target 1). Although the Discussion notes MSA viability/suitability and full bodies of Smaby (2007), Cividini-Motta and Ahearn (2013), and Fiske et al. (2015) remain unavailable (without inferring invisible findings), the current study does not manipulate social-consequence forms or prompt-dependency differential reinforcement (tokens-plus-praise vs. either alone). Likewise, the verified complete Leon, Borrero, and DeLeon (2016; 10.1002/jaba.311) primary manuscript tests parametric post-response time delays (0-120 s) under FR-1 food/token/exchange schedules, whereas Fiske et al. (2019) compare response-based FR-5/10 yoked schedules only as a post-hoc mechanistic contrast. By contrast, Fiske et al. (2019) explicitly design their MSA evaluation to re-test Fiske et al. (2015; 10.1002/jaba.207, verified via abstract and reference list, 'Assessing the value of token reinforcement for individuals with autism')—replacing lengthy progressive-ratio schedules and directly corroborating Fiske et al.'s (2015) empirical findings on token-versus-primary reinforcement efficacy and low unpaired/no-backup token responding.
